q: At which L does the empirically observed small-instance query scaling (alpha ~ 0.124 in our L in {16..1024} data) crossover to the theoretical asymptote alpha = 0.5 for Duerr-Hoyer on trellis-Hamming metric arrays?
basis: Our log-log fit over L in {16..1024} gave alpha = 0.124, far below 0.5. Neither the paper nor the Duerr-Hoyer 1996 paper predicts numerical constants; running the sweep out to L ~ 2^18 on statevector or L ~ 2^30 on a metric-array-only classical simulation of the oracle would identify the true crossover regime.
next_steps: Extend scaling_sweep.py to L up to 2^20 (metric arrays fit in RAM as int32); fit a two-parameter model q = c*L^alpha + d and see whether alpha rises toward 0.5. Compare against uniformly-random metric arrays as a control.

q: How does the QVA behave when the received codeword sits at or below Viterbi's error-correction threshold (t = (d_free-1)/2 = 2 for the (7,5) code), i.e. when the ML path is NOT the transmitted message?
basis: We injected 3 BSC errors (just above t=2) and Viterbi still decoded correctly. As p_flip rises, the ML path diverges from the transmitted message, and it is unclear whether the QVA amplitude-amplification concentrates on the true ML path or on a spurious near-ML path.
next_steps: Sweep p_flip in {0.02, 0.05, 0.10, 0.15, 0.20}, run 200 trials per p_flip, compare (a) classical Viterbi bit-error rate vs true message, (b) QVA argmin correctness vs classical Viterbi. If (b) diverges from 100% before (a) does, that is a novel finding.

q: Does the paper's specific phase-marking + multiphase-kickback amplitude-amplification give tighter empirical constants than plain Duerr-Hoyer minimum finding on the same trellis metric array?
basis: We implemented the standard DH+BBHT wrapper, not the paper's specific G_F^N operator with the Meyer-Pommersheim multiphase kickback (paper section around eq. after line 143). A head-to-head numeric comparison would sharpen the paper's own headline constants -- the paper claims O(sqrt(L)) but does not report measured constants.
next_steps: Implement the paper's G_F^N as a real statevector operator (still O(L) classical work per query) and rerun the same L-sweep. Compare mean-query curves and success rates.

q: How does the query scaling change under an AWGN channel with soft-decision (log-likelihood-ratio) branch metrics instead of Hamming distances over BSC?
basis: Real convolutional decoders in modern communications systems use soft-decision Viterbi. The paper is written channel-agnostic (branch metric is 'a function of the path probability') but does not exercise soft metrics. Soft LLRs give a fundamentally different metric distribution (continuous, Gaussian tails) than integer Hamming distances.
next_steps: Extend encode() to include BPSK modulation over an AWGN channel at various SNRs; replace bin(...).count('1') branch metrics with squared-Euclidean or log-domain LLR sums; rerun L-sweep and check whether alpha and constants change.

q: How does the quantum minimum-finding behave when the metric array has many degenerate minima (equally-likely ML paths)?
basis: Our small-L single-run trials all had unique argmins. For long-frame decoding under moderate noise, ties in integer Hamming distance are common. Grover-min tends to return a uniformly random member of the argmin set -- arguably fine for decoding (any ML path recovers the transmitted message with equal probability) but the paper does not analyze this degenerate case.
next_steps: Construct synthetic metric arrays with controllable degeneracy (k equal minima out of L), run DH-min, measure (a) success rate = P(returned index has minimum value), (b) fairness = KL divergence between empirical index distribution and uniform over argmin set.
